drills.q: True or false: SSM Parameter Store SecureString values are stored unencrypted and rely on IAM alone for protection.
drills.a: False -- SecureString values are encrypted at rest via KMS, free at standard tier, same as Secrets Manager's encryption.

drills.q: What's Secrets Manager's flat monthly fee per stored secret?
drills.a: $0.40/secret/month, prorated hourly, plus $0.05 per 10,000 API calls.

drills.q: Is AppConfig a replacement for Parameter Store and Secrets Manager, or a layer on top of them?
drills.a: A layer on top -- it sources data from Parameter Store, Secrets Manager, S3, or its own profiles, and adds canary rollout strategies with automatic rollback.

drills.q: A service fleet of 500 instances polling Parameter Store every 5 seconds starts seeing throttling errors. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: 500 instances / 5 sec = 100 req/sec, exceeding the 40 ops/sec standard-throughput ceiling. Fix: enable higher throughput mode (up to 3,000 ops/sec), understanding this then bills every account-wide API call at $0.05/10k, or reduce poll frequency / add local caching instead.

drills.q: A team wants automatic credential rotation for a self-hosted PostgreSQL instance not covered by Secrets Manager's native RDS/Aurora templates. What do they need to build?
drills.a: A custom rotation Lambda implementing the four-step contract: createSecret (stage new candidate), setSecret (apply to the actual Postgres instance), testSecret (verify it works), finishSecret (promote to AWSCURRENT, demote old to AWSPREVIOUS) -- Secrets Manager provides the framework/orchestration, not the Postgres-specific logic.

drills.q: Why is granting an IAM role read access to /myapp/* instead of /myapp/prod/api/* a real security risk, even within a single AWS account?
drills.a: It grants cross-environment and cross-component access -- a compromised or buggy prod api service could read staging secrets (often with weaker rotation/access hygiene) or other components' credentials it has no legitimate need for. Scope to the narrowest environment- and component-specific prefix.

drills.q: An engineer pushes a feature-flag change via `aws ssm put-parameter --overwrite` directly to production. Name the two capabilities they lose that AppConfig would have provided.
drills.a: No canary/percentage-based gradual rollout with bake time, and no automatic rollback triggered by a CloudWatch alarm breach -- the change is instantly and globally live to every reader on next poll, with no controlled blast radius and no automated recovery path.

drills.q: Calculate the monthly cost of storing 300 static config values in Secrets Manager versus migrating them to Parameter Store SecureString, ignoring API call costs.
drills.a: Secrets Manager: 300 x $0.40 = $120/month ($1,440/year). Parameter Store SecureString at standard tier: $0, assuming each value is under 4KB and total stays under 10,000 parameters and standard throughput isn't exceeded.

drills.q: Design an AppConfig deployment strategy for a high-risk feature flag rollout that needs both controlled blast radius and per-user consistency during the rollout. What two mechanisms do you combine, and why aren't they redundant?
drills.a: A percentage-based canary deployment strategy with defined bake time and a CloudWatch-alarm-triggered auto-rollback (controls blast radius / limits how much traffic sees a bad change before it's caught), combined with entity-based sticky targeting (2026+) keyed on a stable user/session identifier (ensures a given user consistently sees the same flag state throughout the rollout rather than flipping per-request). They solve different problems -- blast radius control vs. rollout consistency -- so both are needed together.

drills.q: A rotation Lambda for a production RDS credential has been silently failing its testSecret step for two months. What's the observable state of the secret during that time, and why didn't it cause an outage sooner?
drills.a: The secret remains on its last successfully-rotated AWSCURRENT credential -- rotation halts before finishSecret runs if testSecret fails, so the currently-working credential is never invalidated. The lack of an outage masked the failure; the real gap is no alerting on the rotation failure itself, only on downstream symptoms that would eventually appear once the credential's max age/expiration policy (if any) forces the issue.

drills.q: Two teams both create a parameter at /shared/db-host with different intended meanings, and a deploy in one service accidentally reads the other team's value. What's the actual root cause and the structural fix?
drills.a: Root cause: ambiguous, non-namespaced path naming with no per-team/per-component scoping under the shared prefix. Fix: enforce strict /{app}/{env}/{component}/{key} namespacing everywhere, including genuinely shared values (e.g. /platform/common/db-host with an explicit owning namespace), rather than an unscoped /shared/ prefix multiple teams write into independently.
